title: What happened?
mission: The frame everything else hangs on: asking what happened, following the answer, and reacting like a native listener. Everyday Arabic — but at real speed, about real things.
sources: Forms cross-checked against Madrasa dictionary and Living Arabic Project (Levantine)
Urban Palestinian koine (Jerusalem/Ramallah); native-speaker review pending — low-confidence items avoided

lessons.title: What happened today?
lessons.canDo: I can ask what happened, follow the basic answer, and ask the follow-up questions — who, when, why.

blocks.body: Every conversation about news — from street gossip to war reporting — runs on one tiny verb: صار, 'it happened.' This lesson installs the question battery you'll use for the rest of the trajectory.

example.en: What happened today?

items.note: Double duty: events happen (صار إشي) and things become (صار غالي — it got expensive).

cognate.note: Same Semitic root, same meaning. A freebie — you already own this verb.

example.en: Did you hear what happened?
Did you see the news yesterday?

items.note: MSA رأى is almost never said on the street — it's شاف everywhere in the Levant.

cognate.note: Sounds like Hebrew חיכה 'waited' — unrelated. حكى is talking, not waiting.

example.en: He talked to me about the situation.

cognate.note: Looks like חבר 'friend' — different root entirely. خبر is news; plural أخبار.

example.en: There's an important piece of news today.

items.note: شو أخبارك؟ — literally 'what's your news?' — is just 'how are you?'

example.en: Seriously? Unbelievable!

items.note: From عن جد — 'in earnest.' The all-purpose 'wait, really?'

cognate.note: Israeli slang borrowed it wholesale. You already use this word — now meet it at home.

example.en: I swear I didn't hear anything.
Nothing happened, calm down.

items.note: Palestinian shibboleth — Lebanese say شي, Egyptians حاجة. From MSA شيء.

cognate.note: Root ḥ-r-m — the sacred/forbidden zone. Hebrew kept the ban (חרם); Arabic حرام 'forbidden' softened into an exclamation of pity.

example.en: What a pity — they lost their house.
Why is it like this? / Why so?

items.note: هيك الوضع — 'that's how things are.' You'll hear it forty times a day.

blocks.title: Did you hear?
blocks.situation: Samer runs into Layla on the street. Something happened downtown this morning.

lines.speaker: سامر
lines.en: Hi Layla, how are you?

lines.speaker: ليلى
lines.ar: أهلين سامر! الحمدلله. اسمع، سمعت شو صار اليوم؟
lines.en: Hey Samer! Fine, thank God. Listen — did you hear what happened today?

lines.speaker: سامر
lines.en: No — what happened?

lines.speaker: ليلى
lines.ar: في مظاهرة كبيرة في وسط البلد، الناس كلها نزلت عالشارع.
lines.en: There's a big demonstration downtown — everyone took to the street.

lines.speaker: سامر
lines.en: Seriously? Why?

lines.speaker: ليلى
lines.ar: بسبب الأسعار. كل إشي صار غالي.
lines.en: Because of the prices. Everything's gotten expensive.

lines.speaker: سامر
lines.en: That's true, wallah. And when was the demonstration?

lines.speaker: ليلى
lines.en: This morning, around ten.

lines.speaker: سامر
lines.en: And who was there?

lines.speaker: ليلى
lines.ar: شباب، كبار، عيلات كاملة... كل الناس.
lines.en: Young people, old people, whole families... everyone.

lines.speaker: سامر
lines.ar: هيك الوضع صعب عالكل. بدي أشوف الأخبار المسا.
lines.en: Yeah — things are hard for everyone. I'll watch the news tonight.

questions.prompt: What happened downtown?
questions.why: ليلى: في مظاهرة كبيرة في وسط البلد.

questions.prompt: Why did people take to the street?
questions.why: كل إشي صار غالي — everything got expensive.

questions.prompt: When did it happen?
Who was there?
questions.why: شباب، كبار، عيلات كاملة — كل الناس.

points.explanation: Past-tense endings are your ear's anchors: -it (I/you m.), -ti (you f.), -u (they). They fly by in speech — train on them now and half of every story unlocks.

examples.en: We heard a loud sound this morning.
People heard the news and went out.

points.explanation: صار before a noun or adjective means 'became': the price-protest sentence كل إشي صار غالي is the pattern. Before an event, it means 'happened'. Context decides — and context comes by ear.

items.en: I didn't hear anything about the demonstration.
You seriously didn't hear the news? Really?

items.story: s-m-ʕ / ש-מ-ע. Identical root, identical meaning. اسمع = שמע! — the app's name is an imperative you already understand.

One ancient root, ḥ-r-m, 'set apart — sacred or forbidden.' Hebrew went to the ban and boycott; Arabic went to حرام 'forbidden,' which softened into 'what a pity.' When you later meet مقاطعة 'boycott,' remember the Hebrew cousin sat here all along.
حكى 'he spoke' sounds like חיכה 'he waited.' If you hear حكى معي and think 'waited for me,' the whole story changes. Different roots — just an acoustic trap.

lessons.title: Where the news comes from
lessons.canDo: I can follow someone describing how they get their news, and name the channels, sites, and people involved.

blocks.body: Before the news itself: the words for who carries it. Channels, sites, journalists, correspondents — and the crucial Palestinian distinction between خبر and إشاعة, news and rumor.

example.en: What channel is the news on?

items.note: Also a Telegram/YouTube channel — same word carries old and new media.

example.en: I read the news on a Palestinian site.

items.note: Double duty in news language: a website — and a physical site (موقع القصف, the site of the strike).

example.en: My father reads the paper every morning.

items.note: Plural جرايد.

example.en: The journalist did an interview with the family.
Al Jazeera's correspondent reported from Gaza.

items.note: Root ر-س-ل 'send' — the one who is sent. Compare رسالة, a message.

example.en: That's not news — that's a rumor.

items.note: Semantic twin of שמועה but a different root: ش-ي-ع is 'to spread.' A rumor is a spread-thing in Arabic, a heard-thing in Hebrew.

cognate.note: Root ṣ-d-q, truth. Arabic: صدّق believe, صديق friend (the true one), صادق honest. Hebrew took it to justice — צדק, צדיק.

example.en: I don't believe everything I hear.

cognate.note: k-ḏ-b = כ-ז-ב, same root, same meaning. Hebrew אַכְזָבָה 'disappointment' is family too — a hope that lied.

example.en: That talk is all lies.
I follow the news on my phone.
The news turned out to be true.

items.note: Sentence-initial صحيح، ... means 'by the way' — صحيح، سمعت شو صار؟

blocks.title: How Umm Mohammad follows the news
blocks.brief: One speaker, calm pace. Listen twice before opening the transcript. A woman describes her morning news routine — and her daughter's media literacy lecture.
preQuestions: How many different news sources does she mention?
Who in the family prefers the newspaper?
What does her daughter warn her about?

transcript.speaker: أم محمد
transcript.ar: أنا بصحى الصبح، أول إشي بفتح التلفون.
transcript.en: I wake up in the morning — first thing, I open the phone.

transcript.speaker: أم محمد
transcript.ar: بشوف تلغرام، في قنوات أخبار فلسطينية كتير.
transcript.en: I check Telegram — there are lots of Palestinian news channels.

transcript.speaker: أم محمد
transcript.ar: بعدين بسمع الراديو وأنا بعمل القهوة.
transcript.en: Then I listen to the radio while I make the coffee.

transcript.speaker: أم محمد
transcript.ar: جوزي بحب الجريدة، بس أنا بقول الجريدة بطيئة.
transcript.en: My husband loves the newspaper, but I say the paper is slow.

transcript.speaker: أم محمد
transcript.ar: كل إشي بصير، بنشوفه عالتلفون أول بأول.
transcript.en: Everything that happens, we see it on the phone as it happens.

transcript.speaker: أم محمد
transcript.ar: بنتي بتقولّي: يما، مش كل إشي عالفيسبوك صحيح!
transcript.en: My daughter tells me: Mom, not everything on Facebook is true!

transcript.speaker: أم محمد
transcript.ar: ومعها حق، في إشاعات كتير هالأيام.
transcript.en: And she's right — there are a lot of rumors these days.

transcript.speaker: أم محمد
transcript.ar: عشان هيك بتابع صحفيين بعرفهم، مش أي حدا.
transcript.en: That's why I follow journalists I know — not just anyone.

questions.prompt: What does she open first in the morning?
Who likes the newspaper?
What's her complaint about the newspaper?
questions.why: الجريدة بطيئة — by the time it prints, the phone already told her.

questions.prompt: Why does she follow specific journalists?

blocks.title: The b- prefix: how habits sound

points.explanation: بصحى، بفتح، بشوف، بسمع، بتابع — the b- prefix marks the habitual present. It's the sound of someone describing their routine. Strip it (أصحى، أفتح) and you have the bare form used after بدّي and لازم.

examples.en: I follow the news every day.
I want to follow new journalists. (no b- after بدي)

items.story: Straight match: k-ḏ-b / כ-ז-ב. And Hebrew hides a poem in the family: אַכְזָבָה, disappointment — what a lie leaves behind.
ṣ-d-q split beautifully: Arabic kept truth personal (صدّق believe, صديق the true friend), Hebrew made it institutional (צדק justice, צדיק the righteous). One root, two moral vocabularies.

lessons.title: Reacting like a native
lessons.canDo: I can catch the reactions in a conversation — surprise, sympathy, worry, hope — in real time, and produce the right one myself.

blocks.body: Half of any Palestinian conversation is the listener reacting: عنجد؟ والله؟ يا حرام... These discourse markers are small, constant, and carry the emotional plot. Learn them and suddenly conversations have a shape.

example.en: Unbelievable what happened today!

items.note: From عقل, mind — 'it doesn't fit in the mind.' Works for horror and for delight.

example.en: Of course I heard — the whole town heard.
Are you sure the news is true?

items.note: Statement and question in one word — tone does the work. أكيد. / أكيد؟

cognate.note: Borrowed into Israeli slang as-is. From ما عليه شي — 'nothing's on it.'

example.en: Never mind — not a problem.

items.en: God protect us (worry about what's coming)

example.en: God protect us from what's coming.

items.note: Exact functional twin of השם ישמור. The worry-formula before news you don't want.

cognate.note: Another full borrowing into Hebrew slang. Covers everything from sincere prayer to polite 'probably never.'

example.ar: إن شاء الله بترجع الكهربا قبل المسا.
example.en: Hopefully the electricity comes back before evening.
If only the situation would change.

items.note: The exact functional twin of הלוואי — wistful, frequent, essential.

example.ar: يا سلام، هاد كل إشي عندهم؟
example.en: Oh wow, that's all they've got?

items.note: Flat tone = sarcasm. You'll need this for Arc 4's political commentary.

example.en: How's the family? — Thank God, all fine.

items.note: Functional twin of ברוך השם — including the resigned shrug version.

example.en: What did you hear? — Nothing at all.

blocks.title: The electricity's out
blocks.situation: Abu Yousef comes home with bad news about the neighborhood. Count the reactions — they carry the whole conversation.

lines.speaker: أبو يوسف
lines.en: Did you hear? They cut the electricity to the whole neighborhood.

lines.speaker: أم يوسف
lines.ar: عنجد؟ يا زلمة لسا حاطّين اللحمة بالفريزر!
lines.en: Seriously? Man, we just put the meat in the freezer!

lines.speaker: أبو يوسف
lines.en: Never mind — maybe an hour and it's back.

lines.speaker: أم يوسف
lines.ar: يا ريت... المرة الماضية ضلّت مقطوعة يومين.
lines.en: If only... last time it stayed out for two days.

lines.speaker: أبو يوسف
lines.en: God protect us.

lines.speaker: أم يوسف
lines.ar: إن شاء الله بترجع قبل المسا.
lines.en: Hopefully it's back before evening.

lines.speaker: أبو يوسف
lines.ar: أكيد بترجع. مش معقول يومين كمان.
lines.en: It'll be back for sure. No way it's two days again.

lines.speaker: أم يوسف
lines.en: Thank God the weather isn't hot.

questions.prompt: A friend sighs «الله يستر» after reading a headline. What are they expressing?
«يا ريت» signals…
options: A wish that probably won't happen

questions.prompt: Your plans fall through and you tell a Palestinian friend. The natural response:
questions.why: معلش is the consolation move — 'never mind, it's OK.'

questions.prompt: «يا سلام» said in a flat, dry tone means…
questions.why: Tone flips it. The ironic version dominates political talk.

items.ar: والله / معلش / إن شاء الله / أهلين
items.story: Israeli Hebrew borrowed its entire casual-reaction layer from Palestinian Arabic. You've been speaking fragments of this dialect for years — the app just turns the direction around.
Not loans but parallel engineering: two religious cultures built the same emotional valves — the worry-formula and the gratitude-shrug — from the same Semitic toolbox.

lessons.title: Where and when?
lessons.canDo: I can place an event — neighborhood, square, roundabout — and its time, caught by ear.

blocks.body: Every report answers two questions before any other: where and when. This lesson is the city's coordinate system — the square, the alley, the roundabout — and the time words that fly by fastest in real speech.

example.en: The square is full of people today.

items.note: Where demonstrations happen — you'll hear it constantly in Arc 2.

example.en: They've lived in the same neighborhood for ages.

items.note: You met it in قطعوا الكهربا عالحارة. Also the quarters of the Old City — حارة النصارى، حارة المغاربة.

example.en: I'm going downtown — need anything?

items.note: وسط البلد = the center of town. البلد can also mean the country — context decides.

cognate.note: Root f-r-q, 'to split.' Arabic: where roads split. Hebrew: מפרק, where the bone splits — a joint. Same shape, same logic.

example.en: Wait for me at the intersection.

cognate.note: Root d-w-r, turning. Arabic made the turning circle of traffic; Hebrew made דור — the turning of generations.

example.en: There's a traffic jam at the roundabout.

items.note: دوار المنارة in Ramallah is THE meeting point — and where the news happens. أزمة = traffic jam.

example.en: The house is next to the pharmacy.

items.note: From جانب 'side.' The everyday glue word of every address you'll ever hear.

items.en: a little; (قبل شوي) a little while ago

example.en: Wait a bit — they're coming.

items.note: شوي شوي — 'slowly, easy now.' قبل شوي — 'just now.' Tiny word, huge mileage.

example.en: I just got back from work.

items.note: From هالوقت 'this time.' Jerusalemites often say هلّأ; villages and the Galilee say إسا. All mean now.

cognate.note: Root b-k-r, 'first.' Arabic kept it on the clock (early); Hebrew sent it up the ladder (בכיר, senior) and into the family (בכור, firstborn).

example.en: It's still early — why are you up?
Yesterday something strange happened in the neighborhood.

items.note: From البارحة. The trio to automate: مبارح، اليوم، بكرا — yesterday, today, tomorrow.

blocks.title: Where are you, man?
blocks.situation: Khaled has been waiting downtown; Marwan is stuck in traffic. A phone call, two place-names per breath — exactly how Palestinians actually give directions.

lines.speaker: خالد
lines.en: Hello Marwan — where are you, man?

lines.speaker: مروان
lines.ar: أنا هلّق عند الدوار، في أزمة سير فظيعة.
lines.en: I'm at the roundabout right now — terrible traffic.

lines.speaker: خالد
lines.en: I've been waiting for you at the intersection for half an hour!

lines.speaker: مروان
lines.ar: معلش، خمس دقايق وبكون عندك. وين بالظبط؟
lines.en: Sorry — five minutes and I'm there. Where exactly?

lines.speaker: خالد
lines.en: Next to the pharmacy, opposite the square.

lines.speaker: مروان
lines.ar: ماشي. ليش بدك تروح عالبلد أصلًا؟
lines.en: Got it. Why do you need to go downtown anyway?

lines.speaker: خالد
lines.ar: بدي أجيب دوا لإمي قبل ما يسكروا.
lines.en: I need to get medicine for my mother before they close.

lines.speaker: مروان
lines.en: It's still early — they close in the evening.

lines.speaker: خالد
lines.ar: مبارح سكروا الضهر! ما حدا بعرف ليش.
lines.en: Yesterday they closed at noon! Nobody knows why.

lines.speaker: مروان
lines.en: OK, OK — I've arrived. I see you!

questions.prompt: Where is Marwan stuck?
questions.why: أنا هلّق عند الدوار — في أزمة سير.

questions.prompt: Where exactly are they meeting?
Why is Khaled downtown at all?
questions.why: بدي أجيب دوا لإمي — medicine for his mother.

questions.prompt: What happened yesterday?
questions.why: مبارح سكروا الضهر — ما حدا بعرف ليش. Noticing unexplained closures is very Unit 1.

blocks.title: Where + you: question words take suffixes

points.explanation: وين glues straight onto person endings: وينك 'where are you,' وينها 'where is she,' وينهم 'where are they.' One word does the work of a whole English sentence — and it opens half the phone calls you'll ever overhear.

examples.en: Where are you, man? I waited an hour!
Where's your sister? I don't see her.
Where are the guys? Did they all leave?

points.explanation: Before and after a verb need ما: قبل ما يسكروا 'before they close,' بعد ما رجعت 'after I got back.' That little ما is unstressed and easy to miss by ear — train on it now.

examples.en: I want to arrive before they close.

examples.ar: بعد ما رجعت من الشغل، سمعت الخبر.
examples.en: After I got back from work, I heard the news.

items.en: I just now got back from work.
The house is next to the pharmacy.
They were here a little while ago.
Yesterday they closed the pharmacy early.

items.story: f-r-q / פ-ר-ק, 'to split.' Arabic: the intersection, where roads split apart. Hebrew: the joint, where the bone does. Same template (maCCaC), same logic, two maps — one of the city, one of the body.
d-w-r is the Semitic wheel. Arabic spun it into the roundabout (دوّار) and the house the family circles back to (دار). Hebrew spun it into דור — generations, turning one into the next.
b-k-r, 'first.' In Ramallah it's early morning; in Jerusalem officialese it's a senior official; in both traditions it's the firstborn (بِكر / בכור). Hear بكير and think 'first hours of the day.'

lessons.title: Who said?
lessons.canDo: I can track who a piece of information came from, and how sure the speaker sounds about it.

blocks.body: In a place where rumors move faster than news, Palestinians constantly mark their sources: who said, according to whom, how sure. This is the lesson where you start hearing certainty itself — the difference between أكيد and يمكن and شكله is the difference between fact and hope.

cognate.note: q-w-l / ק-ו-ל. Arabic turned the voice into the saying (قال); Hebrew kept the voice itself (קול). Every قال you hear is a קול being used.

example.en: What did the correspondent say?

items.note: قال، قالت، قالوا — the reporting verb. With suffixes it compresses: قالّي 'he told me.'

cognate.note: ḥ-s-b, to reckon. Arabic: according to the count (حسب). Hebrew: to think it through (חשב). Accountants on one side, philosophers on the other.

example.en: According to the news, the situation is calm.

items.note: The sourcing word of every news report: حسب مصادر، حسب شهود عيان...

example.en: Maybe tomorrow, maybe in a week.

items.note: The official soundtrack of waiting. Doubled (يمكن... يمكن...) it means nobody knows anything.

example.en: They say they're going to close the street.

items.note: The rumor-frame. Whoever 'they' are, بحكوا إنه... starts half the stories in the حارة.

example.en: An unofficial source spoke to the channel.

items.note: News-register word you'll hear constantly: مصادر طبية (medical sources), مصدر أمني (a security source).

example.en: Listen to this story.

items.note: خبر in house slippers: the street version of a news item, often gossip-adjacent.

example.en: What you're saying is exactly right.

items.note: From ضبط 'precision.' Alone — مزبوط! — it's the satisfying 'exactly!' of agreement.

example.en: Looks like there's a strike tomorrow.

items.note: Literally 'its shape (is).' Bends to its subject: شكلها، شكلهم، شكلك تعبان — 'you look tired.'

example.en: Apparently the news is true.

items.note: From ظهر 'to appear' — what shows on the surface. A notch more confident than شكله.

example.en: Not sure — but that's what I heard.

items.note: Same أكيد root from Lesson 3, negated and stretched. مش متأكدة for a woman speaking.

blocks.title: Umm Samir's story
blocks.brief: A neighbor relays a rumor — and marks, in every single sentence, where the information came from and how much she trusts it. Listen once for the story; listen again ONLY for the source-words: قالت، بحكوا، حسب، شكله، الظاهر، يمكن.
preQuestions: Who first told her the street will be closed?
What is supposedly the reason for the closure?
Who in her family doubts the whole story?

transcript.speaker: أم سمير
transcript.ar: مبارح بالليل، سمعت صوت سيارات كتير بالحارة.
transcript.en: Last night I heard a lot of cars in the neighborhood.

transcript.speaker: أم سمير
transcript.ar: الصبح، جارتي قالت لي إنه رح يسكروا الشارع كله.
transcript.en: In the morning, my neighbor told me they're going to close the whole street.

transcript.speaker: أم سمير
transcript.ar: حسب اللي بحكوا، في حفريات جديدة جنب الدوار.
transcript.en: According to what people are saying, there's new roadwork next to the roundabout.

transcript.speaker: أم سمير
transcript.ar: بس ابني بقول: يما، هاي إشاعة، مش خبر.
transcript.en: But my son says: Mom, that's a rumor, not news.

transcript.speaker: أم سمير
transcript.ar: شكله ما حدا متأكد من إشي.
transcript.en: It seems nobody is sure of anything.

transcript.speaker: أم سمير
transcript.en: Apparently we just have to wait and see.

transcript.speaker: أم سمير
transcript.en: Maybe tomorrow we'll know the whole story.

questions.prompt: What did she hear last night?
Who said the street will be closed?
questions.why: جارتي قالت لي إنه رح يسكروا الشارع.

questions.prompt: What does her son think?
By the end, how sure is anyone about what's happening?
questions.why: شكله ما حدا متأكد من إشي — the whole lesson in one sentence.

points.ar: قال إنه... / بحكوا إنه... / شكله إنه...
points.explanation: Reported information hangs on إنه ('that'). After قال, بحكوا, الظاهر, شكله — the إنه opens the actual content. By ear it's a tiny 'inno' — once you hear it, you know a claim is coming, and that it's secondhand.

examples.ar: قالت لي إنه رح يسكروا الشارع.
examples.en: She told me (that) they're going to close the street.
They say (that) prices are going to come down.

items.story: q-w-l / ק-ו-ל. Arabic turned the voice into speech — قال, he said. Hebrew kept the raw sound — קול, a voice. בת קול, the heavenly echo, and شو قال؟, what did he say?, are cousins.

ḥ-s-b is reckoning. Arabic counts with it (حسب — according to the count; حساب — the bill), Hebrew thinks with it (חשב, מחשבה — and מחשב, the computer). When a news anchor says حسب مصادر, a Hebrew calculator is humming underneath.
خبرية (a little story) sounds uncannily like חבר'ה (the gang). Different roots, pure acoustic trap — unless the خبرية happens to be about the חבר'ה.

lessons.title: Review & free listening
lessons.canDo: I can follow real Palestinian street answers — short, fast, unscripted — and catch the pattern even when I miss words.

blocks.body: Five lessons of asking what happened, sourcing it, placing it, reacting to it. Now the unit keeps its promise: real people, on a real street, answering a real question — no actors, no script, no slowed-down audio. You will miss words. That's the exercise.

questions.prompt: Play the word. What does it mean?
Play the word. What does it mean?
Play the word. What does it mean?
Play the word. What does it mean?
Play the word. What does it mean?
Play the phrase. What is the speaker doing?

items.en: According to the news, the situation is calm today.
Looks like there's a strike tomorrow.

blocks.title: Real street: where are your grandparents from?
blocks.brief: The Ask Project, Ramallah and around: one question, many strangers, real answers in real dialect. The answers are short and patterned — من + a city, sometimes a year. Cities you'll hear pronounced the Palestinian way: يافا، حيفا، اللد، الرملة. The year that needs no explanation: سنة ٤٨.
